newsitem.title: USA: Wildfires blacken 31,000 acres in California.
newsitem.headline: Wildfires blacken 31,000 acres in California.

text.p: Firefighters used every weapon at their command on Thursday to battle two wildfires in central and southern California that have destroyed thousands of acres of forest and scrubland, forced evacuations and threatened hundreds of oil wells.
The fires in Santa Barbara and Ventura counties, both north of Los Angeles, have destroyed more than 31,000 acres (12,550 hectares) since breaking out on Tuesday.

The blaze, in the Santa Maria area of Santa Barbara county, about 150 miles (240 kilometres) northwest of Los Angeles, had blackened 21,000 acres (8,500 hectares) by Thursday morning in a remote area. No homes or structures were threatened, officials said.

In Ventura County, about 50 miles (80 kilometres) northwest of Los Angeles, nearly 2,000 firemen fought a smaller, but potentially more dangerous blaze which by Thursday morning had consumed more than 10,000 acres (4,000 hectares) in an area dotted with hundreds of oil wells.
Officials said several hundred small songbirds had been lost in the blaze in the Sespe Wilderness area of Ventura county.

The wilderness is also a sanctuary for the California Condor, although there was no indication that any of these large rare birds, which are on the endangered species list, had been threatened by the flames.

Ventura authorities evacuated 14 people from a campsite on the shores of Piru Lake on Wednesday night and another 16 people with lakeside homes were ordered to leave on Thursday morning, county fire department spokeswoman Sandy Wells said.
She said only 10 percent of the blaze had been contained but that was enough to halt the fire's march towards the small towns of Fillmore and Piru.
Fire crews in Ventura county were aided by nine water-dropping helicopters and six fixed-wing air tankers.
Three of the choppers were heavy-lift helicopters capable of drenching the flames with 3,000 gallons (11,350 litres) of water at a time.

Because of the rugged, mountainous terrain, firefighters on the ground were unable to reach the flames and were deployed digging firebreaks, setting backfires and trying to contain the blaze, spokeswoman Wells said.

In addition to the heat generated by the blaze, fire crews had to endure temperatures breaking the 100 degree Farenheit (37 degrees Centigrade) mark, a figure not unusual for the area at this time of the year.
Wells said that authorities were concerned about the fate of several hundred small oil wells throughout the Sespe Wilderness.
"We don't see an immediate problem because the wells should be able to withstand the fire, but we want to make sure there will be no problem," she said.
To that end, she added, fire trucks were ready to go out to the wells to protect them. They are owned by small, independent companies.
